title: Magical Staircase: Convert the Final Fork
summary: After the checks create a fork, collect the rook and stop the most urgent passed pawn before assuming the game is finished.

nodes.question: What should White collect after the final queen fork?
nodes.explanation: Qa7 has checked the king and attacked the rook on b6. After Kg6, Qxb6+ takes that rook and reaches a fully reconstructed seven-piece White win; the f3 passer still deserves attention.

branches.title: Independent reply: blockade the dangerous passer
commentary: Begin with Qa7 and Kg6 immediately before the source rook capture. The knight on h7 already captured Black’s queen and was then taken by the king.
Qxb6+ removes the rook with check along the sixth rank. White has Kb3/Qb6/f4/g4 against Kg6/b5/f3: exactly seven pieces and an exact White win.
Kf7 is an independently supplied legal reply to the check. Black cannot play f2 immediately while its king is checked.

Qf2 places the queen directly in front of the f3 passer, stopping its advance. This exact seven-piece position remains a White win; the branch is a representative continuation rather than a recovered game score.

commentary: Compare another legal king escape after the same source rook capture with check.

Kg7 steps off the checked sixth rank. Both b5 and f3 remain, so White still has a conversion to complete.
Qxb5 collects the b-pawn while retaining White f4/g4 and Black f3. The exact six-piece result confirms a White win; the passer is not silently removed or assumed harmless.

exercises.prompt: Why is taking the rook not the end of the thinking?
exercises.answer: Black still has b5 and f3. In the representative Kf7 line White uses Qf2 to stop the f3 passer; the exact outcome is checked after each step.

exercises.prompt: Why are there seven pieces after Qxb6+?
exercises.answer: White has king, queen and two pawns; Black has king and two pawns. The earlier Nxh7 captured Black’s queen, Kxh7 removed White’s knight, and Qxb6+ removes the rook.
